title: Long-term care insurance in New Jersey: claims and appeals
dek: How long-term care insurance works, when a policy starts paying, how to file a claim for a parent, what New Jersey's Long-Term Care Partnership does for Medicaid, how to appeal a denial and how to find a lost policy.
keyFacts: Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care, such as ongoing help with bathing and dressing.
Most newer policies pay when a licensed practitioner certifies a need for help with 2 of 6 daily activities for at least 90 days, or severe cognitive impairment.
New Jersey's Long-Term Care Partnership began July 1, 2008. Each dollar a Partnership policy pays protects a dollar of assets for Medicaid.
Policies lapsed because of cognitive impairment can be reinstated if requested within five months.
Insurance complaints: NJ Department of Banking and Insurance, 1-800-446-7467.
body:
Long-term care insurance helps pay for help with daily life, such as an aide at home, assisted living or a nursing home, when someone can no longer manage on their own. A policy usually starts paying after a licensed professional confirms the person needs help with at least two basic activities, like bathing or dressing, or has a serious cognitive impairment such as dementia. Then a waiting period, often 30 to 90 days, has to pass.

If your mom or dad bought a policy years ago, it may be worth a great deal now. Medicare does not pay for long-term care, so these policies can make the difference between paying out of pocket and getting real help. This guide explains how claims work in New Jersey, what the state's Long-Term Care Partnership means for Medicaid, what to do if a claim is denied, and how to track down a policy nobody can find. It is general information, not legal or financial advice. For your parent's own policy, the insurer, the state Department of Banking and Insurance or an elder law attorney can help.

How does long-term care insurance work?

You pay premiums, often for decades. When you need ongoing help, the policy pays a daily or monthly amount up to a lifetime maximum. It covers the kind of care Medicare and Medigap do not.

Medicare says plainly that it does not pay for long-term care. It covers short stays in a skilled nursing facility after a hospital stay and some skilled care at home, but not ongoing help with bathing, dressing, meals or supervision. People pay for that themselves, through Medicaid if they qualify, or with long-term care insurance. Our guide to what senior care costs in New Jersey shows why these bills add up so fast.

When you read the policy, look for these parts:

  • Daily or monthly benefit. The most it pays per day or month.
  • Benefit period or lifetime maximum. How long it pays, or the total pool of money.
  • Elimination period. How many days of need must pass before benefits start.
  • Inflation protection. Whether the benefit grows each year.
  • Where care can happen. Home care, adult day care, assisted living and nursing homes. Many older policies cover only some of these.
  • How it pays. Most policies reimburse actual costs up to the limit. Some pay a set cash amount for each day you qualify, whether or not you use paid services.

When does a long-term care policy start paying?

Benefits begin after the person meets the policy's benefit trigger and the elimination period has passed. For most policies sold today, the trigger is needing help with two of six daily activities for at least 90 days, or severe cognitive impairment.

The benefit trigger

Federal tax law defines the trigger for "tax-qualified" policies, which most newer policies are. A licensed health care practitioner must certify, within the past 12 months, that the person:

  • cannot do at least two activities of daily living without substantial help, and is expected to need that help for at least 90 days, or
  • needs substantial supervision to protect their health and safety because of severe cognitive impairment.

The six activities are eating, toileting, transferring (getting in and out of a bed or chair), bathing, dressing and continence. New Jersey rules say a policy's trigger cannot be stricter than needing help with three of these, or having a cognitive impairment, and the assessment must be done by a licensed or certified professional such as a doctor, nurse or social worker. Older policies may use different wording, so read your parent's policy itself.

Dementia matters here. A parent who can still bathe and dress may qualify on cognitive grounds alone if they need supervision to stay safe, for example because they wander or leave the stove on. Our guide to life after a dementia diagnosis covers the medical side.

The elimination period

This works like a deductible measured in days. Most policies let buyers pick 30, 60 or 90 days. Your family pays for care during that time. Some policies count only days when paid care was actually received, so keep every invoice from the start.

How do I file a long-term care insurance claim for my mom?

Call the insurance company as soon as your parent starts needing regular help, even before you hire anyone. Ask for a claim packet and the exact rules for the elimination period. Starting early protects days that may count.

  1. Find the policy and call. Use the number on the policy or a premium bill. Have the policy number, your parent's date of birth and their doctor's name ready. If you are calling for your parent, the company will ask for their permission or a power of attorney.
  2. Get the doctor involved. The insurer will want medical records and a statement about which daily activities your parent needs help with, or about their cognitive impairment. Ask the doctor to be specific.
  3. Expect an assessment. The insurer usually sends a nurse or social worker to evaluate your parent at home. Be there. Describe a bad day, not a good one. Many older adults put on their best face for visitors.
  4. Get the plan of care. Once approved, the insurer's care manager sets a plan of care listing the services covered. Ask for it in writing.
  5. Use approved providers. Many policies require a licensed home care agency or facility. Confirm before you hire. Our guides on choosing a home care agency and vetting in-home help show how to check New Jersey registration.
  6. Keep paper on everything. Save invoices and timesheets, write down every call with date, name and what was said, and send forms by a trackable method.
  7. Ask about premium waiver. Some policies stop charging premiums once benefits start. Ask whether your parent's does, and when.

A geriatric care manager can help document needs and deal with the insurer if this is too much to juggle.

What is the New Jersey Long-Term Care Partnership?

It is a state program that links certain policies to Medicaid. If your parent has a qualified Partnership policy, every dollar it pays out lets them keep one extra dollar of assets if they later apply for Medicaid.

New Jersey's Partnership took effect on July 1, 2008. The Department of Banking and Insurance gives this example: a Partnership policy that pays $100,000 in benefits lets the owner protect an additional $100,000 in assets when applying for Medicaid. Those protected assets are also shielded from Medicaid liens and recovery.

A few things to know:

  • Partnership policies sold in New Jersey come with a written Notice of Long Term Care Partnership Status. Look for it in the policy papers, or ask the insurer.
  • Buying a Partnership policy does not by itself make someone eligible for Medicaid. They still must meet the medical and financial rules.
  • Changing the inflation protection can affect Partnership status. Ask the insurer before you change it.
  • Moving to a state without a Partnership program, or one that does not have reciprocity with New Jersey, can change or end the protection.

Our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS explains how Medicaid pays for long-term care in New Jersey. An elder law attorney can tell you how a Partnership policy fits your parent's plan.

What if a long-term care claim is denied?

Ask for the denial in writing, then appeal through the insurer. New Jersey requires every policy to describe how to appeal a benefit decision. If you still disagree, file a complaint with the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance.

  1. Find out exactly why. Ask which activities the insurer says your parent can do alone, or why the cognitive trigger was not met. Ask for a copy of the assessment.
  2. Read the appeal section. Note the deadline and the address.
  3. Build the record. Get a detailed letter from the doctor, notes from aides or family about each daily activity, and any memory testing results. Ask for a new assessment if your parent's condition has changed.
  4. Appeal in writing. Keep a copy and proof of mailing.
  5. Call the state. The Department of Banking and Insurance takes complaints about long-term care insurance. Call the consumer hotline at 1-800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays, or file a complaint online.

For large claims or repeated denials, a lawyer who handles insurance or elder law can review the policy. You can also check that an insurance agent is licensed in New Jersey with the department's license search.

What happens if a premium is missed?

New Jersey has protections against an accidental lapse. Insurers must wait until a premium is 30 days overdue to send a lapse notice, and they must also notify a backup person if one was named.

Under New Jersey rules, buyers have the right to name a third person to get lapse notices, such as an adult child. The notice must go out at least 30 days before the policy ends. If a parent missed payments because of cognitive impairment or loss of function, the policy can be reinstated if the request is made within five months after it ended.

If Dad has dementia, ask his insurer to add you as the person who gets lapse notices.

If the premium has gone up and is hard to afford, call the insurer before you stop paying. Ask what it would cost to lower the daily benefit, shorten the benefit period or change the inflation rider. Keeping a smaller policy often beats losing it. Remember that changing inflation protection may affect Partnership status.

How do you find a parent's lost long-term care policy?

Look for proof of premium payments. A policy that is still being paid for is still in force, and the bank or checkbook will show who is being paid.

  • Check bank statements, the checkbook register and automatic payments for an insurance company name.
  • Look through files, a safe deposit box and mail for premium notices or annual statements.
  • Ask a past tax preparer. Premiums are sometimes listed with medical expenses on a return.
  • Ask former employers, unions and professional groups whether your parent signed up for a group policy at work.
  • Call the agent or financial adviser your parent used.

Once you know the company, call it with your parent's name, date of birth and Social Security number, and permission or a power of attorney. Then put a copy of the policy with your parent's other papers. Our important papers checklist shows what else belongs in that folder. If no policy turns up, Medicaid, the JACC program and veterans benefits are other ways New Jersey families pay for care.

faq.q: How do I file a long-term care insurance claim for my dad?
faq.a: Call the insurer as soon as he needs regular help and ask for a claim packet. You will need his permission or a power of attorney, his doctor's records and a statement of which daily activities he needs help with. The insurer usually sends a nurse or social worker to assess him. Keep every invoice from the start of the elimination period.

faq.q: What triggers long-term care insurance benefits?
faq.a: For tax-qualified policies, a licensed health care practitioner must certify that the person cannot do at least two of six activities of daily living (eating, toileting, transferring, bathing, dressing, continence) without substantial help for at least 90 days, or needs substantial supervision because of severe cognitive impairment. Then the elimination period must pass.

faq.q: Does long-term care insurance cover dementia?
faq.a: Policies generally include cognitive impairment as a benefit trigger. A person with dementia who needs supervision to stay safe may qualify even if they can still bathe and dress. Check the exact wording in the policy.

faq.q: What is a Partnership policy in New Jersey?
faq.a: A long-term care policy that meets the state's Partnership standards. If it pays benefits and the owner later applies for Medicaid, they can keep extra assets equal to what the policy paid, and those assets are protected from Medicaid recovery. Partnership policies come with a written notice of Partnership status.

faq.q: My mom's long-term care claim was denied. What can I do?
faq.a: Get the reason in writing, read the appeal section of the policy and send a written appeal with a detailed doctor's letter and notes on her daily needs. If that fails, file a complaint with the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance at 1-800-446-7467 or online.

faq.q: How can I find out if my parent has long-term care insurance?
faq.a: Look through bank statements, the checkbook and automatic payments for premiums to an insurance company. Check files and mail for annual statements, and ask former employers, unions, a tax preparer or the agent your parent used.

title: Medicare Savings Programs in NJ: QMB, SLMB and QI for 2026
dek: New Jersey can pay your parent's $202.90 Medicare Part B premium, and with QMB most Medicare cost sharing too. Here are the 2026 income and asset limits, what each program covers, and how to apply through NJSave.
keyFacts: QMB, SLMB and QI all pay the Medicare Part B premium, $202.90 a month in 2026.
QMB also covers Medicare deductibles, coinsurance and copays for covered care.
2026 NJ income limits for one person: $15,960 (QMB), $19,152 (SLMB), $21,546 (QI) a year.
Asset limit: $9,950 single, $14,910 couple. The home and one car do not count.
Apply through NJSave or call 1-800-792-9745. Approval brings Extra Help automatically.
body:
New Jersey's Medicare Savings Programs pay Medicare costs for older adults with modest incomes and savings. The most common benefit is the Part B premium, which is $202.90 a month in 2026. That is more than $2,400 a year back in your mom or dad's pocket, because the premium normally comes out of their Social Security check.

There are three programs: QMB, SLMB and QI. In 2026, a single person with income up to $21,546 a year and savings under $9,950 may qualify for at least one of them. You apply once, through the state's NJSave application or your county board of social services, and the state decides which program fits. Anyone who gets into one of these programs also gets federal Extra Help with prescriptions automatically.

What do QMB, SLMB and QI pay for?

All three pay the Medicare Part B premium. QMB, the program with the lowest income limit, also pays Medicare deductibles, coinsurance and copays for covered care.

ProgramWhat it pays
QMB (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary)Part A premium if you owe one, Part B premium, and the deductibles, coinsurance and copays for services Medicare covers
SLMB (Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary)Part B premium only
QI (Qualifying Individual)Part B premium only

Most people get Part A without a premium because they or a spouse worked long enough. So for most families, QMB, SLMB and QI all start with the same thing: the $202.90 Part B premium stops coming out of the Social Security check. Once the state starts paying, the deduction stops and the monthly deposit goes up by that amount.

QMB goes further. Medicare's own rules say providers are not allowed to bill someone in QMB for the deductibles, coinsurance and copays on services and items Medicare covers. For 2026, that means no $283 Part B deductible, no $1,736 Part A hospital deductible and none of the usual 20% coinsurance on doctor visits, as long as the care is covered by Medicare. A small Medicaid copay may still apply.

If your parent's income is low and they are still paying the Part B premium, they are probably leaving money on the table.

What are the 2026 income and asset limits in New Jersey?

For 2026, New Jersey's Division of Aging Services lists annual income limits of $15,960 (QMB), $19,152 (SLMB) and $21,546 (QI) for a single person. The asset limit is $9,950 for one person and $14,910 for a couple.

ProgramSingle, yearly incomeCouple, yearly income
QMBUp to $15,960Up to $21,640
SLMBUp to $19,152Up to $25,968
QIUp to $21,546Up to $29,214
Assets, all three$9,950$14,910

The state's Get Help Paying Medicare brochure says your home and one vehicle are not counted as assets. Bank accounts, savings and investments generally are. If your parent is a little over the line on income, apply anyway. Medicare.gov's national chart shows slightly higher monthly figures than the state's annual list (for example, $1,350 a month for a single person in QMB), because some small amounts of income are not counted. Medicare.gov tells people to apply even if they don't think they qualify.

Check the date on any chart

These limits change every year, and older charts are still online. The figures above are the 2026 numbers from the Division of Aging Services. Confirm with the NJSave hotline at 1-800-792-9745 before you rule your parent out.

Does a Medicare Savings Program come with Extra Help?

Yes. Anyone enrolled in QMB, SLMB or QI automatically gets Extra Help, the federal program that lowers Medicare drug plan costs. In 2026, people with Extra Help pay no more than $12.65 for each drug their plan covers.

Extra Help also removes the Part D late enrollment penalty, according to the state's brochure. For a parent who skipped drug coverage years ago and pays a penalty every month, that alone can matter.

New Jersey adds its own layer on top. PAAD, the state's prescription program, can bring copays down to $5 for generics and $7 for brand names, and it has a much higher income limit ($54,943 single, $62,390 married in 2026). The same NJSave application checks for both. Our guides to PAAD and prescription and bill help show how the pieces fit together.

How do I apply for a Medicare Savings Program in NJ?

Apply through NJSave, New Jersey's single application for older adults and people with disabilities, online or on paper. You can also apply in person at your county board of social services, the office that handles Medicaid.

  1. Gather the numbers. You will need your parent's Social Security and Medicare numbers, their monthly income from every source (Social Security, pensions, IRA withdrawals, part-time wages) and recent statements for bank, savings and investment accounts.
  2. Choose how to file. Fill out the NJSave application online, or call 1-800-792-9745 and ask for a paper copy. If your parent might also need full Medicaid, the county board of social services can look at everything at once. Find your county office through our county pages.
  3. Answer every question. One NJSave form screens for the Medicare Savings Programs, Extra Help, PAAD, Senior Gold, the Lifeline utility credit and hearing aid help. Leaving sections blank slows things down.
  4. Watch the mail. The state may ask for more proof. Answer quickly and keep copies of everything you send.
  5. Check the Social Security deposit. Once your parent is approved, the Part B premium should stop coming out of the check. If it keeps showing up, call the hotline.

If you want a person to walk through it with you, call SHIP, the State Health Insurance Assistance Program, at 1-800-792-8820. SHIP counselors are free and do not sell insurance.

How do I apply for my mom if she can't do it herself?

You can fill out NJSave with your mom and have her sign it, or help her apply at the county board of social services. If you hold power of attorney, bring a copy. Letters from the state go to her address, so plan who will open them.

A few habits make this easier for families:

  • Sit down together. Many older adults prefer to do this on paper or by phone. That is fine. The phone line is there for exactly this.
  • Collect the mail. Approval letters, requests for proof and renewal notices all go to your parent. A missed letter is the most common reason help stops.
  • Be wary of surprise calls. Hang up on anyone who calls out of the blue asking for a Medicare number or bank details to "activate" a benefit, and call the hotline yourself. Our guide to scams targeting older adults covers the common Medicare tricks.

Say your dad, a widower in Union County, gets $1,250 a month from Social Security and has $6,000 in savings. His income works out to $15,000 a year, under the QMB limit, and his savings are under $9,950. If approved, the state would pay his Part B premium and his Medicare cost sharing, and he would get Extra Help with drugs. The same NJSave application would also check him for PAAD and the Lifeline utility credit. This is only an example. The state makes the final call.

Can coverage start before the application date?

Sometimes, for SLMB and QI. Federal rules let SLMB and QI coverage reach back up to three months before the month you apply, if your parent was eligible then. QMB starts no earlier than the month after the state decides your parent is eligible, so it pays to apply soon.

The CMS manual for state programs says the three-month look-back does not apply to QMB, and that QI can't reach back into the previous calendar year. A January application for QI, for example, can't cover the prior December. If your parent was eligible earlier and paid premiums in the meantime, ask about the start date when you apply.

QI has one more wrinkle. Medicare.gov says you must apply every year to stay in QI, and states approve QI on a first-come, first-served basis, with priority for people who had QI the year before. Put the renewal on the calendar.

How do these programs fit with NJ FamilyCare and Medigap?

Medicare Savings Programs are run by the state Medicaid system, but they are not full Medicaid. Someone in SLMB or QI keeps regular Medicare and gets only premium help. Someone with very low income and assets may qualify for full NJ FamilyCare on top of QMB, which covers more, such as some long-term care.

If your parent might need help at home or in a nursing home down the road, read our guides to NJ FamilyCare for older adults and Medicaid long-term care (MLTSS).

If your parent pays for a Medigap policy and qualifies for QMB, the Medigap plan may be paying for costs QMB already covers. Talk with a SHIP counselor before dropping any coverage, because getting a Medigap policy back later is not always possible. People who are new to Medicare can start with our Medicare 101 for New Jerseyans turning 65.

This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice. For your parent's exact situation, call SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 or the NJSave hotline at 1-800-792-9745.

faq.q: How do I find out if my mom qualifies for a Medicare Savings Program in NJ?
faq.a: Compare her yearly income and savings to the 2026 limits: up to $21,546 in income and under $9,950 in assets for a single person, with the home and one car not counted. If she is close, apply anyway through NJSave or call 1-800-792-9745. The state decides which program fits.

faq.q: What is the difference between QMB and SLMB?
faq.a: QMB has the lowest income limit and pays the Part B premium plus Medicare deductibles, coinsurance and copays for covered care. SLMB allows a little more income but pays only the Part B premium.

faq.q: Does a Medicare Savings Program include Extra Help with prescriptions?
faq.a: Yes. Anyone in QMB, SLMB or QI automatically gets Extra Help. In 2026 that means no more than $12.65 for each drug a Medicare drug plan covers.

faq.q: How do I apply for my dad if he can't fill out the forms?
faq.a: Fill out the NJSave application with him online or on paper and have him sign it, or go with him to the county board of social services. Bring a copy of your power of attorney if you have one, and make sure someone reads the letters the state mails to him.

faq.q: Do I have to reapply every year?
faq.a: QI must be renewed every year, and states approve it first come, first served, with priority for people who had it the year before. Watch for renewal notices for any program and answer them quickly.

faq.q: Can a Medicare Savings Program pay for months before I applied?
faq.a: SLMB and QI can reach back up to three months before the month you apply if your parent was eligible then, though QI can't go back into the prior calendar year. QMB starts no earlier than the month after the state decides your parent qualifies, so apply as soon as you can.

title: The $250 senior property tax deduction in NJ: who qualifies
dek: Homeowners 65 and older, or disabled, with very low income can take $250 a year off their New Jersey property tax bill. Here is how the $10,000 income limit works, how to file Form PTD with your town, and the March 1 form that keeps it.
keyFacts: $250 a year off the property tax bill for qualifying homeowners 65+, disabled, or surviving spouses 55+.
Income limit: $10,000 a year for you and your spouse, after leaving out Social Security or one government pension.
File Form PTD with your town's tax assessor (Oct. 1 to Dec. 31) or tax collector (during the tax year).
File Form PD5 with the tax collector by March 1 every year, or the deduction is billed back.
Separate from ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ. You can get it on top of them.
body:
New Jersey takes $250 a year off the property tax bill of homeowners who are 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, if their income is very low. The income limit is $10,000 a year for the homeowner and spouse combined, but you can leave out Social Security or one kind of government pension when you add it up.

You apply with Form PTD at your town's tax assessor or tax collector, not with the state. Then you file a short income statement, Form PD5, by March 1 every year to keep it. This is a separate benefit from ANCHOR, the Senior Freeze and Stay NJ, so your mom or dad can get it on top of those.

Who qualifies for the $250 senior property tax deduction?

Homeowners who are 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, by December 31 of the year before the tax year, and whose income stays at or under $10,000 after one permitted exclusion. They must also own and live in the home and have lived in New Jersey for at least a year.

Here is the full list from Form PTD and the Division of Taxation. "Pretax year" means the year before the tax year you are claiming.

  • Age or disability. Age 65 or older as of December 31 of the pretax year, or permanently and totally disabled and unable to work as of that date.
  • Residence. A legal resident of New Jersey for at least one year immediately before October 1 of the pretax year. The form's instructions say U.S. citizenship is not required.
  • Ownership. You owned the home and lived in it as your main residence as of October 1 of the pretax year. Vacation and second homes do not count.
  • Income. You reasonably expect your income, plus your spouse's or civil union partner's, to be no more than $10,000 for the tax year, after the exclusion described below.
  • One per home. Only one deduction is allowed per home, no matter how many qualified people live there.

Owners of a unit in a cooperative or mutual housing corporation can apply too. The form has a section for resident shareholders.

What counts as income for the $10,000 limit?

Nearly everything counts, except you may leave out one of three things: Social Security benefits, a federal government retirement or disability pension, or a state, county or municipal government retirement or disability pension. You pick one category, not all three.

Form PTD says income includes wages, tips, interest, dividends, rents, business income, capital gains and, in full, pensions, annuities and retirement benefits. They count even if they are partly or fully exempt from federal income tax. The gain from selling your own main home is not counted. Income of other family members living in the house, such as a grown child, is not counted. Only the homeowner and spouse.

An example

Say your mom is 78, widowed and owns her house in Paterson. She gets $22,000 a year from Social Security and $4,000 in bank interest and IRA withdrawals. She leaves out Social Security, so her countable income is $4,000. She is under $10,000 and may qualify. If she also had a $9,000 private company pension, her countable income would be $13,000, and she would not. This is an example only. Your assessor decides.

Because the limit is so low, this deduction mostly helps older adults whose money comes almost entirely from Social Security or a public pension. If that sounds like your parent, it is worth asking about, even though the $250 is modest.

Can a surviving spouse or a disabled homeowner get it?

Yes. A disabled homeowner of any age can qualify with proof of disability. A widow or widower can keep the deduction if they were at least 55 when their spouse died, are 55 or older now, have not remarried, and live in the same home that got the deduction.

For disability, the Division of Taxation accepts a physician's certificate or a Social Security document, and the form also lists a New Jersey Commission for the Blind certificate.

For a surviving spouse, the Division lists these conditions:

  • The deceased spouse or civil union partner was receiving the senior or disabled deduction on this same home when they died.
  • You were 55 or older when they died, and you are 55 or older as of December 31 of the pretax year.
  • You have not remarried or formed a new civil union.
  • You have owned and lived in the home for at least a year before October 1 of the pretax year, and you meet the same income limit.

After a death, families have a long list of calls to make. Add the tax assessor to it, so the deduction moves to the surviving spouse instead of being dropped. Our guide on what to do when a parent dies has the rest of that list.

How do I apply for my mom or dad?

Fill out Form PTD and bring it, with copies of your proofs, to the town's tax assessor between October 1 and December 31 of the year before the tax year. Or file it with the tax collector at any point during the tax year itself.

  1. Get the form. Download Form PTD from the Division of Taxation, or ask for one at town hall. Many town tax offices keep copies at the counter.
  2. Find the right office. The assessor and collector are municipal offices. The state keeps a list of local tax assessors, and your town website lists the collector.
  3. Gather proof. The Division lists documents such as a birth certificate, the deed, a New Jersey driver's license, a state tax return, a physician's certificate or Social Security document for disability, and a death certificate and marriage certificate for a surviving spouse. Bring copies, and ask the office ahead of time what they want to see.
  4. Sign it. Your parent signs as the owner. The statements are made under penalty of perjury, so the income figures need to be honest estimates.
  5. Look for it on the bill. Once approved, the $250 shows up as a deduction on the property tax bill.

Timing example: for the 2027 tax year, your parent can file with the assessor from October 1 to December 31, 2026, or with the tax collector any time during 2027. A parent who turned 65 during 2026 and meets the other rules can start the 2027 claim right now.

What is the PD5 form, and what happens if we miss March 1?

Form PD5 is the Annual Post-Tax Year Income Statement. You must file it with the tax collector on or before March 1 every year to confirm last year's income stayed under the limit. If it is late, the deduction is disallowed and your parent is billed for the $250.

Some towns, such as Wall Township, mail the form to people with the deduction in January, but do not count on it. Put March 1 on the calendar every year. This is the step families miss most easily, especially when a parent's mail piles up or the adult child handles the bills from another town.

If the assessor or collector denies the application, you can appeal to your County Board of Taxation. The Division of Taxation says to file Form A-1 on or before April 1 following the denial.

Getting the deduction takes one form. Keeping it takes one more form every March 1.

How is this different from ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ?

The $250 deduction comes off the property tax bill through your town, and it has a very low income limit. ANCHOR, the Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are state programs, handled by the Division of Taxation through one application, the PAS-1, with much higher income limits.

ProgramWho runs itIncome limitHow you get it
$250 senior or disabled deductionYour town's assessor and collector$10,000, after excluding Social Security or one government pensionForm PTD, then Form PD5 every March 1
ANCHORNJ Division of TaxationMuch higher, see our ANCHOR guidePAS-1 application
Senior FreezeNJ Division of TaxationMuch higher, see our Senior Freeze guidePAS-1 application
Stay NJNJ Division of TaxationMuch higher, see our Stay NJ guidePAS-1 application

The PAS-1 filing deadline for 2025 benefits was November 2, 2026. For the next application and its deadline, check the Division of Taxation's property tax relief page. For most older homeowners, those state programs are worth far more than $250, so don't skip them. The property tax relief hotline is 1-888-238-1233. See our guides to property tax relief in New Jersey, ANCHOR, the Senior Freeze and Stay NJ.

What about the $250 veterans deduction?

Honorably discharged veterans with active duty service who own their New Jersey home can get a separate $250 deduction, filed with the assessor on Form V.S.S. A surviving spouse may be able to claim it too. It is based on military service rather than age. Our guide to benefits for older veterans explains who qualifies and what to bring. A parent who is a veteran and also meets the senior rules should ask the assessor about both deductions at the same visit.

This guide is general information, not tax or legal advice. Your town's tax assessor decides each claim, and the Division of Taxation's property administration office answers general questions at 609-292-7974. If money is tight overall, our guide to prescription and bill help covers programs with far higher income limits.

faq.q: How do I get the $250 property tax deduction for my mom?
faq.a: Fill out Form PTD with her and file it, with copies of proof of age, ownership and residency, at her town's tax assessor between October 1 and December 31, or with the tax collector during the tax year. Then make sure the Form PD5 income statement goes to the tax collector by March 1 each year.

faq.q: Does Social Security count toward the $10,000 income limit?
faq.a: No, if you choose to exclude it. You may leave out one of three categories: Social Security, a federal government pension, or a state, county or municipal government pension. Everything else, including private pensions, IRA withdrawals and interest, counts in full.

faq.q: Can my dad keep the deduction after my mom dies?
faq.a: He may, if your mom was getting the deduction on that home, he was 55 or older when she died and is 55 or older now, he has not remarried, and he meets the income limit. Tell the tax assessor about the death and ask what proof they need.

faq.q: What happens if we forget the March 1 PD5 form?
faq.a: If the Form PD5 is not filed on time, the deduction is disallowed and your parent is billed for the $250. Put March 1 on the calendar every year.

faq.q: Is this the same as ANCHOR or the Senior Freeze?
faq.a: No. The $250 deduction is handled by your town and has a $10,000 income limit. ANCHOR, the Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are state programs with much higher income limits, applied for on the PAS-1. A parent can get all of them.

faq.q: Can a veteran get both the senior deduction and the veterans deduction?
faq.a: The veterans deduction is a separate $250 deduction based on military service, filed on Form V.S.S. A parent who is a veteran and also meets the senior rules should ask the tax assessor about both.

title: Social Security offices in NJ: appointments and online help
dek: How to find your Social Security office in New Jersey, make an appointment, skip the trip online, what to bring, and how to help a parent with forms and payees.
keyFacts: Find your office at ssa.gov/locator by ZIP code. The national number is 1-800-772-1213, weekdays 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time.
Social Security asks for appointments at field offices but says it will not turn away people who can't make one.
In fiscal year 2026, people with an appointment waited about 6 minutes on average, versus a combined average just under 21 minutes.
A power of attorney does not let you manage a parent's benefits. You must apply to be their representative payee.
Social Security never asks for sensitive information by text, email or social media. Report scams at oig.ssa.gov/report.
body:
To find your Social Security office in New Jersey, enter your ZIP code in the Social Security office locator on ssa.gov. It shows the nearest office's address, phone number and hours. Social Security asks you to make an appointment before you go, either online or by calling 1-800-772-1213 weekdays from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Many people never need to visit an office. You can apply for retirement or Medicare, change your address or direct deposit, request a replacement card in many cases and print a benefit letter from home with a free my Social Security account. If you are helping a parent, there are specific forms that let you speak for them or manage their payments, and they matter more than a power of attorney does at Social Security.

How do I find my local Social Security office in NJ?

Use the office locator at ssa.gov/locator and search by address, city or ZIP code. Your office is assigned by where you live, so use your parent's ZIP code if you are looking up their office.

The locator lists each office's street address, phone numbers, hours and a link to temporary closings. In some areas it also shows a Card Center, which handles only new or replacement cards and record updates. Offices sometimes close for weather or building problems, so check the locator or the closings page the morning you go. You can also find your office's address through the automated menu on the national number.

We don't list New Jersey office addresses here. Offices move, close and change hours, and an out of date address costs you a trip. The locator is the official source.

Do I need an appointment at a Social Security office?

Yes, in most cases. Since January 6, 2025, Social Security has asked people to schedule an appointment for service in its field offices, including for cards. The agency says it will not turn away people who can't or won't make one.

In its notice about the change, Social Security said vulnerable people, military personnel, people with terminal illnesses and others who need immediate help can still walk in. Still, an appointment saves time. In figures updated October 1, 2026, Social Security reports that for fiscal year 2026, the average combined wait in field offices was just under 21 minutes, and people with an appointment waited about 6 minutes on average. Your office may be faster or slower.

  1. Schedule online. Go to ssa.gov and choose "Make or change an appointment." You answer a few questions, and Social Security may tell you the task can be done online. Your appointment may be by phone or in person.
  2. Or call. Call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) weekdays, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., and say you want to schedule an appointment. Help is available in English, Spanish and other languages.
  3. Save the confirmation. To change or cancel, use the link in the confirmation email or text. If a representative booked it, you also need the code they gave you.

Phone help has gotten faster too. Social Security reported an average speed of answer of half a minute on the national number in August 2026, down from 9 minutes a year earlier. The agency says waits tend to be shorter in the morning, later in the week and later in the month. Automated phone services run 24 hours a day.

What can I do online instead of going in?

Most common tasks. You can apply for benefits on ssa.gov, and a free my Social Security account covers most of the rest. Some tasks also work through the automated phone line.

  • Apply for retirement, disability or Medicare.
  • Check the status of an application or appeal.
  • Change your address or direct deposit.
  • Request a replacement Social Security card. In many cases this can be done online, and the card arrives by mail in 5 to 10 business days. A local office cannot print one for you.
  • Print a benefit verification letter or a replacement SSA-1099 tax form.
  • Get your Social Security Statement and check your earnings record.
  • Name up to three people who could manage your benefits if you ever can't (more on that below).

To open an account, you verify your identity through Login.gov or ID.me. Login.gov, the usual choice in the United States, needs an email address, a government photo ID and a phone number. If you get stuck, call 1-800-772-1213 and say "Help Desk" for priority help. If the computer is the hurdle, our guide to free tech help in New Jersey lists classes and libraries that can sit with you.

Turning 65 soon? Social Security handles Medicare sign-up for most people. Our Medicare 101 guide explains the timing, and our page on the 2027 Social Security raise covers what changes in January.

What should I bring to a Social Security appointment?

Bring original documents or copies certified by the agency that issued them. Social Security does not accept photocopies or notarized copies of documents like a birth certificate.

For a retirement application, Social Security says it may ask for:

  • Your Social Security card or a record of the number.
  • Your original birth certificate, a certified copy or other proof of age.
  • If you were not born in the United States, proof of citizenship or lawful status. Expired documents aren't accepted.
  • A copy of military service papers if you served before 1968. A photocopy is fine.
  • A copy of last year's W-2 forms or self-employment tax return. A photocopy is fine.

If Social Security already has your proof of age or citizenship from an earlier claim, you don't need to bring it again. Documents are returned to you. And if something is missing, Social Security says not to delay applying, because waiting could cost benefits. The local office can sometimes verify a birth record with the state at no cost.

Bring your appointment confirmation, a list of questions, and something to write on. If you are going with your mom or dad, bring the forms described in the next section.

How do I help my mom or dad with Social Security?

It depends on what kind of help they need. There are three main tools, and each does something different.

SituationWhat to use
Your parent wants you to be able to get information about their record.Your parent gives written consent. Form SSA-3288 is the standard paper form. A parent 18 or older can also submit an electronic consent online for certain records, but they have to do it themselves after verifying their identity.
Your parent has a claim or appeal and wants someone to act on it.Form SSA-1696, Claimant's Appointment of a Representative. The representative can be a lawyer or a non-attorney. A representative can't charge a fee unless Social Security authorizes it first.
Your parent can no longer manage their own benefit payments.Apply to become their representative payee with Form SSA-11. Social Security usually requires the payee interview face to face.

Power of attorney is not enough. Social Security says a power of attorney, a joint bank account or being an authorized representative does not give you legal authority to manage someone's benefits. If your parent can't manage the money, you must apply and be appointed as payee.

What a payee does. A payee uses the benefits for the person's current needs, like housing, food and medical care, saves what is left, keeps records and reports changes such as a move. A payee can't sign legal documents other than Social Security papers, and individual payees can't charge a fee. Spouses no longer have to file the annual payee report but still must keep records.

Plan ahead. A parent who is still able can name up to three people in advance who could serve as payee if the need ever comes up. They can do this in their my Social Security account or by calling 1-800-772-1213. It is not a power of attorney, and Social Security still checks the person when the time comes.

These choices fit alongside a will, health care proxy and power of attorney. Our guides to estate planning and guardianship explain how the pieces work together. This is general information and not legal advice. A legal aid office or elder law attorney can help with a specific situation.

How do I spot a Social Security scam?

Social Security will never ask for sensitive information by social media, email or text. Its scam page warns that scammers insist on gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency or cash because those are hard to trace. Hang up on anyone who threatens to suspend your number or have you arrested.

Social Security's inspector general lists four signs of a scam. The caller pretends to be from an agency you know. They say there is a problem or a prize. They pressure you to act now. They tell you to pay in a specific way.

Scammers often spoof real government phone numbers, use the names of real employees and send photos of badges. They may say you need to pay or confirm information to receive a cost-of-living increase. Real raises happen automatically.

  • Pause, hang up and don't click links.
  • Call Social Security yourself at 1-800-772-1213 if you're unsure.
  • Report it to the Social Security Office of the Inspector General at oig.ssa.gov/report.
  • If money was taken, call your local police. The Federal Trade Commission takes reports at 1-877-382-4357, and you can press 3 to speak with an interpreter.

Opening a my Social Security account also protects your parent, because no one else can open one in their name, and you get an alert if someone tries to change the address or direct deposit. See our guide to scams aimed at older adults in New Jersey for the latest tricks.

Where else can I get help with benefits?

Social Security handles retirement, disability, SSI and Medicare enrollment. For help paying Medicare costs, look at state programs too.

Our guide to Medicare Savings Programs in New Jersey explains how the state can pay the Part B premium for people with limited income. For free one-on-one Medicare counseling, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program at 1-800-792-8820. And for a parent's other benefits, the county Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 is a good first call.

faq.q: How do I make an appointment at the Social Security office for my mom?
faq.a: Call 1-800-772-1213 weekdays from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. and say you want to schedule an appointment, or use the appointment tool on ssa.gov. Have her name, Social Security number and the reason for the visit ready. It helps if she is with you on the call.

faq.q: Can I walk in to a Social Security office in New Jersey without an appointment?
faq.a: Social Security asks for appointments, but it says it will not turn away people who are unable or unwilling to make one. Expect a longer wait without one.

faq.q: How do I talk to Social Security on behalf of my dad?
faq.a: Your dad can give written consent with Form SSA-3288, or submit an electronic consent himself online. If he has a claim or appeal, he can appoint you with Form SSA-1696. If he can no longer manage his payments, you would apply to be his representative payee.

faq.q: Does Social Security accept a power of attorney?
faq.a: Not for managing benefit payments. Social Security says a power of attorney does not give authority to manage someone's Social Security or SSI benefits. You must apply and be appointed as representative payee.

faq.q: What can I do online with my Social Security account?
faq.a: On ssa.gov you can apply for retirement, disability or Medicare. With a my Social Security account you can check a claim's status, change your address or direct deposit, request a replacement card in many cases, print a benefit letter or SSA-1099 and review your earnings record.

faq.q: Is a call from Social Security about my COLA real?
faq.a: Be very careful. Social Security says scammers claim you must pay or share information to get a cost-of-living increase. Raises are applied automatically. Hang up and call 1-800-772-1213 yourself.

title: How to appeal a property tax assessment in NJ
dek: Deadlines, filing fees, the Chapter 123 ratio test, what evidence counts, and how a win can change Senior Freeze and Stay NJ. A plain guide for older homeowners and the families helping them.
keyFacts: Most appeals must reach the County Board of Taxation by April 1 (May 1 after a town-wide revaluation or reassessment).
Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth counties use a January 15 deadline.
County board filing fees run from $5 (assessed under $150,000) to $150 ($1 million or more).
You appeal the assessed value, not the taxes. Value is judged as of October 1 of the prior year.
Use up to five comparable sales. Neighbors' assessments are not accepted as evidence.
body:
If you think the town has your home valued too high, you can appeal the assessment to your County Board of Taxation. For most New Jersey homeowners the petition must be received by April 1 of the tax year, or by May 1 in a town that just finished a town-wide revaluation or reassessment. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth counties use an earlier calendar, with a January 15 deadline.

You do not appeal the tax bill itself. You appeal the value the assessor put on the property, and you have to prove what the home was worth on October 1 of the year before. The filing fee is small, from $5 to $150 at the county board. The work is in the evidence. This guide walks through how it works, with a family helping an older parent in mind. It is general information, not legal or tax advice. For advice on a specific case, see the last section for who can help.

When is the deadline to appeal a property tax assessment in NJ?

For 2027 taxes, most appeals must reach the county board by April 1, 2027. In Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth counties the date is January 15, 2027. In a town that put in a revaluation or reassessment, it is May 1.

A few details matter here:

  • Received, not postmarked. The state's Form A-1 instructions say the appeal must be received by the county board, not just mailed. One that arrives after closing time on the last day is dismissed as late.
  • The later date wins. If your town mails its assessment notices late, you get 45 days from the date the bulk mailing was completed, if that falls after April 1 (or January 15 in the three early counties).
  • Weekends and holidays. If the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day.
  • A changed assessment. If the assessor sends a Notification of Change of Assessment, you have 45 days from that notice.

The town mails the assessment notice as a postcard. In Burlington and Gloucester it goes out in November of the year before. Elsewhere, state law says it must be mailed before February 1. If your mom or dad's mail piles up, or you handle the bills from another town, watch for that card. It shows the assessed value you would be appealing.

What about an added assessment after a renovation?

If your parent finished an addition or other improvement after October 1, the town can send an added assessment for the rest of the year. Appeals of added and omitted assessments use a different form, the AA-1. It must be received by December 1, or 30 days after the town mails the added or omitted tax bills, whichever is later. Check your county board's page if one of these arrives this fall.

How do I know if my parent's assessment is too high?

An assessment is too high if it is above what the home would have sold for, after you adjust for your town's average ratio. The test the boards use is called Chapter 123, after the 1973 law that created it.

Most New Jersey towns do not assess homes at 100% of market value. Each year the state Division of Taxation studies sales in every town and sets an average ratio, the typical relationship between assessments and sale prices. The county board then allows a range of 15% of that ratio either way. This is the common level range. The ratio changes each October 1 for use in the next tax year, and the Division of Taxation posts it for every town.

If your parent's assessment, divided by the home's true market value, lands inside that range, the board will not change it. If it lands above the upper limit, the board lowers the assessment to the average ratio times the market value. If it lands below the lower limit, the board must raise it.

Say your mom's town has an average ratio of 80%. The range runs from 68% to 92%. Here is how three homes worth $400,000 would come out.

AssessmentRatio to $400,000 valueWhat the board does
$380,00095%, above 92%Lowers it to $320,000 (80% of $400,000)
$350,00087.5%, inside the rangeNo change
$260,00065%, below 68%Raises it to $320,000

An assessment can look high and still be fair under the law. In a town that just had a revaluation, the ratio is treated as 100%, so the question is simply whether the assessment is more than the home was worth.

An appeal is a fight about value, so start by asking what the house would really have sold for last October.

Where do I file a tax appeal, and what does it cost?

Almost every homeowner files with the County Board of Taxation in the county where the property sits. If the property is assessed at more than $1,000,000, the owner may file directly with the Tax Court of New Jersey instead.

You file the original Form A-1 with the county board. The instructions also require a copy to the town's tax assessor and a copy to the municipal clerk, with the same attachments. Many county boards take appeals online. Burlington and Gloucester, for example, both offer online filing. Your county board's website will say how it works there.

Assessed valueCounty board filing fee
Less than $150,000$5
$150,000 to less than $500,000$25
$500,000 to less than $1,000,000$100
$1,000,000 or more$150

Fees are not refundable. There is no fee to appeal a denied senior citizen or disabled person deduction, or a denied veteran deduction. If the town turned down your parent's $250 deduction, see our guide to the senior property tax deduction.

To keep the appeal alive, your parent must keep paying taxes. The law requires all taxes and municipal charges due through the first quarter of the current year to be paid. Do not hold back the bill while you wait for a decision.

What evidence do I need for a tax appeal hearing?

The best evidence is recent sales of similar homes nearby. The board presumes the assessment is correct, so it is on your parent to show, with facts, what the home was worth.

  1. Get the property record card. Ask the town tax assessor's office. It lists what the town thinks your parent owns: square footage, rooms, baths, garage, finished basement. Mistakes here are worth fixing.
  2. Pick up to five comparable sales. The rules allow no more than five. For each, list the block, lot, sale price and deed date. Look for sales close to the October 1 assessment date, in the same neighborhood, with similar size, age, style and lot.
  3. Check that the sales are usable. The state's comparable sales form says to use open market sales between willing buyers and sellers. A sale between relatives, for example, is a poor choice. The county board and the assessor can show you sales records.
  4. Skip your neighbors' assessments. The instructions are blunt about this. Comparable assessments are not acceptable evidence of value. Only sales count.
  5. Add photos. Pictures of a leaking roof, an old kitchen or a busy road next door help explain why the home is worth less.
  6. Send everything on time. If the comparables were not attached to the petition, they must reach the assessor, the clerk and the board at least seven calendar days before the hearing.

An appraisal is allowed, but it comes with rules. The written report must be in at least seven days ahead, and the appraiser has to come to the hearing to testify. If your parent bought the home recently, the form asks for the price and date. The Monmouth County board notes that a recent sale price is not always conclusive proof of value.

What happens at the hearing, and after?

A panel of county board commissioners hears the case, usually in a short session open to the public. The town is the other side, often with its assessor or attorney. By law, the board must hear and decide appeals within three months of the filing deadline.

The homeowner has to be there, or be represented by a New Jersey attorney. The appeal form also lets your parent choose a summary hearing, decided only on the papers sent in. That can help if travel is hard, though an appraisal brings the appraiser and the owner back to the hearing. An adult child can usually come along for support. If the property is in a trust or an LLC, the rules on who may appear are stricter, so read the instructions or call the board.

Three things families should know going in:

  • Do not miss the hearing. Adjournments are granted only for extraordinary reasons. If nobody shows up, the board can dismiss the case for lack of prosecution, and the state warns that this may keep it from going on to the Tax Court.
  • The town can cross appeal. The municipality may ask the board to raise the assessment. As the table above shows, an assessment below the range can go up.
  • A settlement still needs approval. If the assessor offers a deal before the hearing, it goes on the board's form and the board must approve it.

If you disagree with the result, you can appeal to the Tax Court within 45 days from the date the judgment was mailed. If you accept a county board judgment and do not appeal, the Freeze Act generally holds the assessment for that year and the next two, unless something big changes, such as a town-wide revaluation or an added assessment. The Tax Court is at the Hughes Justice Complex in Trenton, 609-815-2922.

How does a tax appeal affect Senior Freeze and Stay NJ?

A win lowers your parent's tax bill, and that can change the state relief checks. Call before you file so there are no surprises.

Senior Freeze pays back increases above a base year amount. The Division of Taxation says that if your property taxes are reduced because of a reassessment or appeal, it may adjust your base year to the new amount. Stay NJ is also figured from your property taxes, and the state says total relief can never be more than the taxes paid on the home. So a lower bill can shrink those payments too.

None of this is a reason to skip a strong appeal. A lower assessment lowers the bill every year it lasts. But the numbers can shift, so ask the Senior Freeze information line at 1-800-882-6597 or the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 how a change would play out. Our guides to Senior Freeze, Stay NJ and all the property tax relief programs explain the formulas.

Keep filing the relief forms

An appeal does not replace the PAS-1 application for ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ, or the yearly form that keeps the $250 deduction. Keep those on the calendar too.

Where can my parent get help with a tax appeal?

Start with the free sources. The county board's staff can explain filing and deadlines, though they cannot argue the case for you. The town assessor's office can walk you through the property record card.

  • County Board of Taxation. Every county has one. The Division of Taxation keeps a statewide contact list, and our county pages point you to local offices.
  • Legal Services of New Jersey. Free civil legal help for people with low incomes. Call 1-888-576-5529.
  • A private attorney. Tax appeal lawyers handle these regularly, and an elder law attorney can help when the appeal is part of a bigger plan, such as a move or a trust.
  • A licensed appraiser. Worth it when the gap is large. Remember the appraiser must testify.

If you are helping from a distance, put the key dates on your own calendar: the assessment postcard (mailed before February 1 in most towns), the April 1 deadline (January 15 in Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth) and December 1 for added assessments. Keep a folder with the record card, your comparable sales and the board's letters. For help with income tax returns, see our guide to free tax help.

faq.q: What is the deadline to appeal property taxes in New Jersey?
faq.a: For most homeowners the appeal must be received by the County Board of Taxation by April 1 of the tax year, or 45 days after the town's assessment notices were mailed if that is later. Towns with a new revaluation or reassessment have until May 1. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth counties use January 15.

faq.q: How much does it cost to file a property tax appeal in NJ?
faq.a: At the county board the fee depends on the assessed value: $5 under $150,000, $25 from $150,000 to under $500,000, $100 from $500,000 to under $1 million, and $150 at $1 million or more. Appeals of a denied senior, disabled or veteran deduction are free.

faq.q: How do I appeal the property tax assessment for my mom's house?
faq.a: Your mom, as the owner, files Form A-1 with the county board by the deadline, with copies to the town assessor and clerk. You can gather comparable sales, fill out the form with her and go with her to the hearing. She must attend or be represented by a New Jersey attorney, unless she chooses a summary hearing decided on the papers.

faq.q: Can a tax appeal raise my parent's assessment?
faq.a: Yes. The town can cross appeal, and if the board finds the assessment is below the low end of the common level range, it must raise it. Check the numbers before you file.

faq.q: Will winning an appeal affect my dad's Senior Freeze?
faq.a: It can. The Division of Taxation says it may adjust the Senior Freeze base year when taxes drop because of an appeal or reassessment, and Stay NJ is also figured from property taxes. Call the Senior Freeze line at 1-800-882-6597 or the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 before filing.

faq.q: Do we have to keep paying property taxes during the appeal?
faq.a: Yes. State law requires all taxes and municipal charges due through the first quarter of the current year to be paid for the appeal to go forward. Keep paying the bills on time.
